You use the particle CI for places (ci vado, ci abito) and the particle NE for quantities (ne compro due, non ne ho) and in expressions like "che ne pensi?".
of it, of them; about it
Are you going to the market? — Yes, I'm going now.
How many eggs would you like? — I'll take six.
Have you got any boxes? — No, I haven't got any.
It takes three hours to move.
What do you think of the new flat?
To replace a place with CI: Vai a Roma? — Sì, ci vado.
To use NE for quantities: Quanti ne vuoi? Ne voglio tre.
To say "none" with NE: Non ne ho.
To use NE for "about / of it": Che ne pensi? Non ne so niente.
To use CI VUOLE / CI VOGLIONO for time and things you need.
To make the participle agree with NE: Ne ho comprate due (bottiglie).
At the market, before the party
Friday morning at the Sant'Ambrogio market. Tomorrow Giulia is moving, and on Sunday she's having a party in the new flat. She and Matei are buying everything.
Good morning! What can I get you?
I'd like some tomatoes. Are they good?
Excellent, madam! How many would you like?
I'll take two kilos. And some basil.
Basil… sorry, I haven't got any left today. It ran out at eight.
Never mind. Graziella has loads on her terrace. I'll pop round tonight.
The eggs are very fresh. Would you like a dozen?
No, six will do. Matei, how many people are coming on Sunday?
Let's see… Graziella, Pietro, Signor Franco, the colleagues… I think twelve are coming. And your brother?
Gennaro? He's coming tomorrow from Naples in his car. It takes him four hours, if there's no traffic.
In the little red car? And how many boxes will fit in it?
Not many. But we've got thirty… It'll take three trips!
You're moving? Then here's a crate of strawberries for you, on the house. For the new home!
Thank you so much! What do you say, Matei, shall we come back here every Friday?
"che ne dice" = what do you say (about it)
CI = "chee", CE = "che", as in Romanian: "ci vado", "ce n'è". Not "kee"!
SC + a = "sk": SKA-to-la, SKA-le. SC + i/e = "sh" (uscire).
ZZ = a long "dz": dod-DZEE-na. Also in "mezzo" (MED-dzo).
Careful: in "fragole" the G and L are separate (FRA-go-le). GL is read as a soft "ly" only before I (figli).
CI replaces a place already mentioned, usually introduced by a, in, da, su. It goes before the verb, like a pronoun.
Sì, ci sono stato a novembre.
You already know it from "c'è / ci sono" (there is / there are). "Ce" appears before "ne": "Quanti scatoloni ci sono? — Ce ne sono trenta."
NE replaces a noun when you state a QUANTITY of it. The number or amount stays after the verb:
You can't leave the quantity without NE: "Quanti fratelli hai? — Ho uno" is wrong. Correct: "Ne ho uno." In Romanian we simply say "am unul", but Italian needs NE.
The difference: "Le uova? Le prendo tutte." (I'll take them all — direct) ≠ "Le uova? Ne prendo sei." (I'll take six of them — quantity).
NE also replaces a phrase with "di": "parlare di", "pensare di", "sapere di", "avere bisogno di":
Do you need help? — Yes, I need it.
"Me ne vado!" = "I'm off!" — a very common expression that we'll understand better with double pronouns (chapter 20).
4. CI VUOLE / CI VOGLIONO and CI METTO
"Ci vuole" has the thing needed as its subject: "Ci vuole pazienza" (it takes patience), "Ci vogliono due ore". "Ci metto" has the person as its subject: "Gennaro ci mette quattro ore."
As with lo / la / li / le, the participle agrees with the noun NE replaces (when it's a quantity):
How many bottles did you buy? — I bought two.
How many books have you read? — I've read five.
How much pasta did you eat? — I ate too much!
Are you going to Siena? — Yes, I'm going tomorrow.
How old are you? — I'm thirty.
Have you got any bread? — No, I haven't.
Have you ever been to Rome? — Yes, I've been twice.
What do you think of the film?
It takes two hours to get to Bologna.
How many photos did you take? — I took a hundred!
How many boxes are there? — There are thirty.
"How many brothers have you got? — One."
On Saturday morning at seven Gennaro arrived from Naples in the little red car. "It took me three and a half hours," he announced proudly. "A record." Nobody wanted to know how fast he'd driven.

In the old flat on via dei Serragli there were thirty boxes, a sofa, a bed, a bookcase and an enormous plant called Totò. "How many boxes will fit in your car?" Matei asked. Gennaro looked at the mountain of cardboard. "Six will fit. Maybe seven, if Totò travels on the roof."

Luckily the reinforcements arrived. The colleagues from the workshop came with a borrowed van. Signor Franco brought a wooden cart from 1960. Pietro brought his energy, which was worth three grown men.

The real problem was the new flat: fourth floor, no lift, with narrow, steep stairs. Matei carried the first box up, very pleased with himself. By the tenth he was no longer pleased. By the twentieth he had stopped talking.

"What's in this box? Bricks?" asked Gennaro, as red as a tomato. "Art books," Giulia replied. "How many have you got?" "I don't know… I've bought a lot." Gennaro counted: nine boxes of books. "Sister, you don't even read half of them!"

The sofa was the hardest part. It wouldn't go through the door, it wouldn't turn on the stairs. It took forty minutes, six people and a lot of words in Neapolitan that Matei didn't understand, but which Pietro learned at once.

By six in the evening everything was inside. They were dead tired, sitting on the floor among the boxes. Then someone knocked at the door. It was Graziella, who had climbed up slowly, one step at a time, with a pot of ribollita and a bunch of basil. "I've made enough for an army," she said. "Eat."
They ate on the terrace, watching the dome turn pink at sunset. Totò the plant was at last in its place, in a sunny corner.

Gennaro raised his glass. "To my sister's new home. And to the next move: let's hope there's a lift." Then he looked at Matei, who had fallen asleep against a box of books. "And let's hope you do the next move together. Then he can carry the books up."
Giulia went red. Matei, luckily, was asleep and didn't hear a thing.
Quanto ci ha messo Gennaro da Napoli?
Che cosa c'era negli scatoloni più pesanti?
Qual è stata la parte più difficile?
How many brothers have you got? — Two.
It takes a lot of time.
I don't know anything about it.
Have you been to Siena? — Yes, I went yesterday.
It takes me twenty minutes to get to work.

Wine: I've already got six bottles, but Gennaro is bringing four more from Naples.
